name: Sidaama
confidence_why: Kawachi 2013, the author of the Sidaama reference grammar, states first-hand that Sidaama is a pitch accent language in which high pitch marks prominence and the accusative-oblique case, and the other sources differ only in framing: Hudson 1989 calls it 'stress' and offers a hedged HEC-wide default (final long vowel, otherwise penult) with marked exceptions, Moreno 1940 found the accent too mobile to state a rule, and Appleyard 1991 reports the accent as phonemic with a morphological role, so the type is secure but rests on one modern fieldworker's short statement and no full phonology of the language was read.

catalog_quote: Kawachi 2013: 573: "Sidaama is a pitch-accent language, which indicates prominence with high pitch." ... "Sidaama nouns inflect for case, gender and also for the 'Unmodified/Modified' distinction (see below), and use a suprafix (employing high pitch) in addition to suffixes. ... Sidaama uses suffixes for the nominative, dative-locative, allative, and ablative-instrumental cases, a suprafix for the accusative-oblique case, and both for the genitive case." || Hudson 1989: 6 (Word stress): "In all five HEC languages there appears to be a general rule of stress on word-final long vowels and (rarely) diphthongs, and stress on the vowel of the next-to-last syllable when there is no word-final long vowel or diphthong. I have not indicated stress which is consistent with this rule (including in words from Sasse 1982), but stress is marked where this general rule is violated, for example not uncommonly on word-final short vowels. It is possible that stressed word-final vowels are phonemically long; presumably they are historically so."
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress goes on the final syllable if it contains a long vowel or diphthong; otherwise on the penultimate syllable. Deviations (stress on a final short vowel) are lexically marked and may reflect underlying/historical final length. Stated as a generalization over all five HEC languages including Sidamo, not for Sidamo alone.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress 'not uncommonly' on word-final short vowels, marked individually in the dictionary; author suspects such vowels are phonemically (historically) long. Older source Moreno 1940 (pp. 18-19, saved) says the accent is very unstable, shifts within the phrase, and cannot be reduced to rules. Kawachi (BLS 2007: 260 n. 2, saved) treats the system as pitch: accusative case is marked by high pitch on the stem-final vowel, i.e. accent is partly morphological.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; dictionary citation forms (nouns cited in the accusative, verbs as stems). Hedged ('there appears to be'). The modern primary description (Kawachi 2007 dissertation; Anbessa Teferra 2000/2014) describes Sidaama as a pitch accent language and would supersede this.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted Hudson 1989 rule is stated for all five Highland East Cushitic languages jointly (Burji burj1245, Gedeo gede1246, Hadiyya hadi1240, Kambaata kamb1316, Sidamo sida1246), not for Sidamo specifically; Hudson's Sidamo data are from his own fieldwork (dictionary based on Sidamo, Gedeo, Hadiyya, Kambata plus Sasse's Burji). Modern work (Kawachi 2007 and later) treats Sidaama as a pitch accent language in which some high pitches are morphological (e.g. accusative = high pitch on stem-final vowel), so 'stress' here should be read as pitch accent. Moreno 1940 describes the northern Sidamo of the Italian-era Sidamo Commissariat (same language, older data).

new_statements.quote: Sidaama is a pitch-accent language, which indicates prominence with high pitch. [...] Sidaama nouns inflect for case, gender and also for the 'Unmodified/Modified' distinction (see below), and use a suprafix (employing high pitch) in addition to suffixes. Sidaama has a nominative-accusative case system (Kawachi, in press b). Sidaama uses suffixes for the nominative, dative-locative, allative, and ablative-instrumental cases, a suprafix for the accusative-oblique case, and both for the genitive case.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing statement's type (pitch accent; catalog records Hudson 1989 as 'pitch accent'). It gives no placement rule, so it neither confirms nor contradicts Hudson's 'final long vowel, else penult' rule; it adds that high pitch on a word-final short vowel is the accusative-oblique marker, which is exactly the class of rule-violating final-short-vowel stress Hudson 1989 says he marks individually. Hence 'refines'. Earlier line placed this statement at Section 1 p. 571; corrected here to Section 3 p. 573.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prominence is realized as high pitch (a pitch accent system). No default placement rule is given. Accent is morphologically active: the accusative-oblique case is marked by a high-pitch suprafix on the noun's final vowel (farašš-ó 'horse.ACC' vs farašš-u 'horse-NOM.M', p. 574), and the genitive uses both a suffix and the suprafix (isé '3SG.F.GEN', p. 575).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; the case-marking suprafix means accent position on a noun varies with case (final vowel high in the accusative-oblique).
new_statements.identity_note: Kawachi 2013 describes Sidaama as spoken in the Sidaama Zone, South-Central Ethiopia, from the author's consultants and transcribed folk tales; no dialect is named. Hudson 1976 is a chapter on Highland East Cushitic as a group (Sidamo, Hadiyya, Kambaata, Alaba, Burji), not Sidaama alone. The Kawachi 2007 and 2008 entries are the same dissertation (SUNY Buffalo PhD; UMI print edition).

new_statements.quote: Stress is phonemic in at least four of the HEC languages, but seems to involve contrasts only in final syllables. As a general rule, stress is predictable, falling on "strong" syllables -- syllables with long vowels, and/or closed syl- lables. [...] S. meesane ‘ax! is pronounced méésane [...] However, in four of the languages, final open syllables of some words are stressed, in contravention of the general rule. [...] Occasionally in Sidamo, and in at least two environments in Kambata, stress has grammatical significance. Two Sidamo illustrations are: (i) the 3rd. m.sing. perfect verb in final i contrasts with the sing. imperative in final i: tami "he asked,' contrasts by stress with t'a?mi

new_statements.relation_note: Differs from what is held by the project in both type and placement. Type: Hudson 1976 describes HEC/Sidamo prominence as (partly phonemic) STRESS, whereas the catalog record (classification tonal; Kawachi 2013: 573 'pitch accent language, which indicates prominence with high pitch') and Kawachi 2007: 63-64 (who cites these very pages and rejects the stress analysis) code it as pitch accent. Placement: Hudson 1976's general rule puts stress on heavy ('strong') syllables wherever they are (S. méésane 'ax' with initial/antepenultimate stress), while Hudson 1989: 6 (statement held by the project) gives penultimate stress unless the word ends in a long vowel/diphthong and Kawachi 2007/2013 give…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Highland East Cushitic generally (Sidamo included): stress is predictable and falls on 'strong' = heavy syllables (long vowel and/or closed), e.g. Sidamo meesane 'ax' pronounced méésane, Hadiyya Sokkisukko with stress on the first (closed) syllable, so it is left unmarked; stress is contrastive only in word-final syllables: in four of the five languages some words carry stress on a final open syllable against the rule (marked with an acute; a Sidamo example is given), and in Sidamo stress occasionally has grammatical value: 3m.sg. perfect in final stressed -i vs. sg. imperative in final -i (tami 'he asked' vs 'ask!'), and 3m.sg. present perfect -ino > -nó vs. 1pl jussive -no (ag- 'drink': 'he has drunk' vs ango 'let's drink').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress in the recovered text of sec. 5.1.2.
new_statements.exceptions: (a) Lexical: 'in four of the languages, final open syllables of some words are stressed, in contravention of the general rule' and only these final stresses are marked (examples for Burji c'ii?á 'bird', k'ubé 'finger-ring'; Darasa mundé 'blood', boobilá 'elephant'; Hadiyya none; Kambata only Amharic loans e.g. oroobá 'Wednesday'; Sidamo one example, scanned-garbled 'seeda ronan jila' with footnote 8); (b) grammatical: 'Occasionally in Sidamo, and in at least two environments in Kambata, stress has grammatical significance': Sidamo 3m.sg. perfect -í vs sg. imperative -i (tami 'he asked' vs t'a?mi 'Ask!'), 3m.sg. present perfect -ino/-né vs 1pl jussive -no (ango 'let's drink'); Kambata infinitives in -i vs imperatives in -i (fuli 'Go out!').
new_statements.identity_note: Kawachi 2007 describes Sidaama (Sidaamu Afoo) as spoken in the Sidaama Zone, southern Ethiopia, from his own fieldwork; Hudson 1976 is a comparative sketch of the five Highland East Cushitic languages (Sidamo, Darasa/Gedeo, Hadiyya, Kambata-Alaba, Burji) in which Sidamo is one of the languages treated.

However, there are those verb suffixes whose final vowel segments are always accented [...]. Such suffixes include: simple perfect (3SG.M: -i, 3SG.F/3PL: -u, 2PL: -i), present perfect (3: -ino, 2PL: -oonni), imperfect (3: -anno, 2PL: -anni), and connective (-e: all persons/numbers/genders) suffixes (Hudson 1976: 248). new_statements.relation_note: Same author and same analysis as the catalog's Kawachi 2013 quote (pitch accent language, prominence = high pitch, accusative-oblique suprafix): the dissertation supplies the placement rule the catalog record lacks (default high pitch on the penultimate vowel segment/mora of the citation form) and the morphological final-accent cases (case suprafix; accented verb suffixes with minimal pairs). Compatible with Hudson 1989's 'penult, or word-final long vowel' stress rule held by the project, which Kawachi restates in moraic terms (first mora of a final long vowel = penultimate vowel segment); it differs from Hudson only in calling the prominence pitch accent rather than stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sidaama is analysed as a pitch accent (not stress) language with predictable accent: in citation forms (and in the nominative, and in predicate position before =ho/=te) high pitch falls on the penultimate vowel segment (= penultimate mora, so the second half of a long vowel/VV sequence in a heavy penult, and the first half of a word-final long vowel); high pitch shifts to the stem-final vowel as a case suprafix in the accusative, genitive and oblique, before noun suffixes, and on a closed list of verb suffixes (3SG.M/3SG.F-3PL/2PL simple perfect, present perfect, imperfect; connective -e), yielding minimal pairs such as ha'r-i 'he left' vs ha'r-i 'leave!' that differ only in accent position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; a single high-pitch accent per word (sec. 2.3.3 adds sentence-final intonation effects on the main verb).
new_statements.exceptions: Words with word-final long vowels (hunkee 'sweat', rodoo 'sibling', meaa 'woman') look final-accented under a syllable analysis but are regular under the mora analysis (accent on the first mora of the final long vowel, p. 65-66); accusative/genitive/oblique nouns, adjectives and pronouns carry final high pitch as a suprafix (p. 69-70, Table 2.3); listed verb suffixes are always final-accented (p. 70, citing Hudson 1976: 248); adverbs usually penultimate (fn. 16); before dative/locative -ho/-te and other noun suffixes high pitch falls on the stem-final vowel (fn. 13, 15).
new_statements.identity_note: Kawachi 2007 describes Sidaama (Sidaamu Afoo) as spoken in the Sidaama Zone, southern Ethiopia, from his own fieldwork; Hudson 1976 is a comparative sketch of the five Highland East Cushitic languages (Sidamo, Darasa/Gedeo, Hadiyya, Kambata-Alaba, Burji) in which Sidamo is one of the languages treated.

new_statements.quote: pp. 63-64: "As far as I know, studies on Sidaama have all assumed that it is a stress language, where “stress” usually falls on the penultimate “syllable” of a word (Hudson 1976: 248-249, Wedekind 1980: 137-140, Abebe Gebre-Tsadik 1985, Teferra 2000: 16). However, this does not seem to be correct in two respects [...]. First, Sidaama is actually a pitch-accent language, where prominence is indicated by high pitch, rather than stress. The location of high pitch in a word is predictable, and high pitch is not associated with the duration of a vowel. [...] In Sidaama, high pitch is normally assigned to the second to the last vowel segment of the citation form of an open-class word."

tone_statements.citation: Frosini, Benedetta. 2008. Tone and case in Sidaamu Afo: a contibution [sic] towards understanding the relationship between tone and the three basic cases (nominative, genitive and accusative) in Sidaamu Afo. MA thesis, Universitetet i Oslo (University of Oslo).
tone_statements.quote: Sidaamu Afo is not being attested as a lexical tone language in the literature. ... I ended with a broad definition of tonal language: the presence of morphemes realized with tonal variations is enough to define a language as a tonal language. ... There is a tonal difference between nom.U and gen.U. The difference rests on the last vowel of the stem of the noun ... while the tone is falling in nom.U, it is high in gen.U. ... I found evidence for the use of tonal contrasts to mark the contrast between nom.U and gen.U case in Sidaamu Afo.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2.1.5 p. 17.. ch. 2 summary pp. 21-22.. sec. 6.1 p. 98 with Table 12 p. 99.. sec. 6.4 p. 101
tone_statements.summary: F0 study of case marking: not a lexical tone language, but tonal in a broad (grammatical) sense; nominative vs genitive differ by a falling vs high tone on the stem-final vowel; no tone inventory.

readall_conflicts: No placement contradiction among the sources actually read, but the framing differs. Hudson 1989 (existing statement, held by the project) speaks of word 'stress' with a general rule for all five HEC languages: stress on a word-final long vowel or (rarely) diphthong, otherwise on the penultimate vowel, with rule-violating cases marked individually, 'not uncommonly on word-final short vowels'. Kawachi 2013 (opened here) calls Sidaama a pitch accent language with prominence realized as high pitch, gives no default placement, and shows accent doing morphological work (a high-pitch suprafix on the final vowel marks the accusative-oblique, e.g. farašš-ó ACC vs farašš-u NOM), which is compatible with Hudson's noted exceptions. Moreno 1940 (held by the project, not in this works list) says the accent in Sidamo is very unstable, shifting within the phrase for psychological and rhythmic reasons, and cannot be fixed in rules at the present state of knowledge. Appleyard 1991 (held by the project) reports from Bender (ed.) 1976 p. 248, inside Hudson's 1976 chapter, that stress is phonemic in at least four HEC languages, with Sidamo minimal pairs; that chapter itself could not be opened. So the sources agree that Sidaama has a culminative word-level prominence realized by pitch, but disagree on whether it is rule-governed (Hudson 1989), lexically/morphologically distinctive (Hudson 1976 via Appleyard; Kawachi 2013), or unstable (Moreno 1940).

sources.quote: Stress is phonemic in at least four of the HEC languages, but seems to involve contrasts only in final syllables. As a general rule, stress is predictable, falling on "strong" syllables -- syllables with long vowels, and/or closed syl- lables. [...] S. meesane ‘ax! is pronounced méésane [...] However, in four of the languages, final open syllables of some words are stressed, in contravention of the general rule. [...] Occasionally in Sidamo, and in at least two environments in Kambata, stress has grammatical significance. Two Sidamo illustrations are: (i) the 3rd. m.sing. perfect verb in final i contrasts with the sing. imperative in final i: tami "he asked,' contrasts by stress with t'a?mi

sources.quote: Sidaama is a pitch-accent language, which indicates prominence with high pitch. [...] Sidaama nouns inflect for case, gender and also for the 'Unmodified/Modified' distinction (see below), and use a suprafix (employing high pitch) in addition to suffixes. Sidaama has a nominative-accusative case system (Kawachi, in press b). Sidaama uses suffixes for the nominative, dative-locative, allative, and ablative-instrumental cases, a suprafix for the accusative-oblique case, and both for the genitive case.

sources.quote: pp. 63-64: "As far as I know, studies on Sidaama have all assumed that it is a stress language, where “stress” usually falls on the penultimate “syllable” of a word (Hudson 1976: 248-249, Wedekind 1980: 137-140, Abebe Gebre-Tsadik 1985, Teferra 2000: 16). However, this does not seem to be correct in two respects [...]. First, Sidaama is actually a pitch-accent language, where prominence is indicated by high pitch, rather than stress. The location of high pitch in a word is predictable, and high pitch is not associated with the duration of a vowel. [...] In Sidaama, high pitch is normally assigned to the second to the last vowel segment of the citation form of an open-class word."

sources.note: Accent in Sidamo, as in other Cushitic languages and Amharic, is 'molto incostante', shifting position within the phrase for psychological reasons and rhythmic combinations, with tendencies like those he described for Galla (Oromo) but not reducible to rules at the present state of knowledge; marked in the grammar where observed to prevail, mostly not marked in the lexicon. Also: accented vowels tend to lengthen, unaccented to shorten; long accented vowels written with circumflex (p. 18); a stressed vowel immediately before an enclitic/suffix geminates its consonant (p. 21).

sources.citation: Frosini, Benedetta. 2008. Tone and case in Sidaamu Afo: a contibution [sic] towards understanding the relationship between tone and the three basic cases (nominative, genitive and accusative) in Sidaamu Afo. MA thesis, Universitetet i Oslo (University of Oslo).
sources.quote: Sidaamu Afo is not being attested as a lexical tone language in the literature. ... I ended with a broad definition of tonal language: the presence of morphemes realized with tonal variations is enough to define a language as a tonal language. ... There is a tonal difference between nom.U and gen.U. The difference rests on the last vowel of the stem of the noun ... while the tone is falling in nom.U, it is high in gen.U. ... I found evidence for the use of tonal contrasts to mark the contrast between nom.U and gen.U case in Sidaamu Afo.

sources.note: Argues Cushitic 'pitch accent' languages are (restricted) tone languages in Hyman's 2006 typology, not stress languages (no obligatoriness), with culminative/demarcative pitch and a distinctive function of tone at the grammatical rather than lexical level. On this language: 'Sidaama has pitch accent (high tone) on the penultimate mora which moves to the ultimate mora in morphology (Kawachi 2007: 63-71)', set beside Kambaata (one accented syllable per word, Treis 2008) and Gede'o (final stress, Dawit 2019).
sources.venue: Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus (SPiL Plus)
